strengths: Addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: enabling frozen VLA models to act on user-specific personal objects among visually similar distractors, a setting distinct from category-level generalization.

The proposed VAP framework is training-free and immediately deployable: a new personal object can be registered with only ~5 reference images and no per-object fine-tuning, which is practically attractive.

Broad and diverse evaluation spanning two new simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER on Google Robot/WidowX, Personalized-VLABench on Franka) and a real-world SO-101 setup with eight object categories and both selection and pick-and-place tasks.

Large and consistent improvements in many settings (e.g., pen-holder SR 8.5%→60.3% and CMR 10.5%→89.2%; WidowX Task 5 CMR 100%/SR 95% with VAP vs. 79.2%/62.5% for Soft Prompt), with the CMR metric usefully separating instance grounding from end-to-end task success.

Thorough and honest failure analysis: a three-way error taxonomy (single-view grounding error, multi-view inconsistency, correct-prompt-but-manipulation-failure) that correctly disentangles perception errors from policy limitations and informs future work.

Good efficiency analysis showing VAP adds only ~10% per-step wall-clock overhead (SAM2 tracking 0.02s vs. VLA inference 0.20s), and detailed reproducibility information (hardware, training data construction, hyperparameters).

The appendix provides a thoughtful investigation of the token-learning baseline, including an embedding-space comparison between PaliGemma and the VLAs and an attention analysis, strengthening the argument that the token baseline is a genuine (not strawman) competitor.
weaknesses: Modest methodological novelty: VAP is essentially a composition of off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO, DINOv2 matching, SAM2 tracking, semi-transparent highlight), closely resembling prior visual-prompting-for-control work (MOKA, PIVOT, TraceVLA, RoboGround) applied to a new personalization setting.

No ablation study isolating the contribution of each component (reference-based grounding vs. visual highlight vs. instruction rewrite). It is unclear whether the gains come from the personalized matching or simply from highlighting a detected object; a 'highlight without reference matching' control would be informative.

The instruction-rewriting component is underspecified and possibly redundant: the template 'my X' → 'the tint-color X' (e.g., 'the red cup') is not clearly justified, and it is unclear how the color is chosen or what happens when the object is not the assumed tint color. Since the highlight already marks the region, the language rewrite may contribute little and should be ablated.

Baseline fairness is limited. The Soft Prompt/token-learning baseline is a proxy transferred from a VLM (PaliGemma) into the VLA rather than trained end-to-end in the VLA; the authors themselves acknowledge the token embedding space shifts (π0.5 cosine 0.9456, kNN@1 ~0.99) and that end-to-end token training was not performed, so the claim that VAP 'outperforms token-learning' is weaker than stated.

Gains are inconsistent across tasks: on Personalized-VLABench, VAP only modestly exceeds the best prompt baseline on cat figurine (51.6 vs. 44.4), miniature house (52.4 vs. 39.6), and cup (60.8 vs. 54.8), and on the bottle task in Personalized-SIMPLER language-only hard prompts are competitive. This suggests the method's advantage is concentrated in a subset of settings and is not analyzed.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance for the real-world experiments, which use only 20 trials per task; several simulation numbers are reported without error bars, making it hard to assess whether some differences are meaningful.

Scope is narrow (single personalized object, short-horizon, tabletop scenes) and depends on the reliability of open-vocabulary detection/segmentation; the paper acknowledges this but the practical reach is limited.
Reproducibility is partial: no statement of code/benchmark release, and the benchmarks rely on specific Sketchfab 3D assets and hardware setups that would be difficult to replicate exactly.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem—personalized manipulation of user-specific objects among visually similar distractors—that existing VLA benchmarks largely ignore, and formalizes it clearly (given K≈5 reference images, act on the specific instance with a frozen policy).

VAP is genuinely simple and training-free: it leaves VLA parameters untouched and only preprocesses inputs, so a new personal object can be used immediately after registration without per-object fine-tuning. The efficiency analysis (Table 5) shows the added per-step cost is small (~0.02s SAM2 tracking vs. 0.20s VLA inference, ~10% overhead).

Substantial empirical effort: two new simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER with Google Robot and WidowX; Personalized-VLABench with Franka, 3 views) plus a real-world SO-101 benchmark spanning 8 categories and both selection and pick-and-place tasks (Table 1, Figure 2).

Consistently large reported gains over generic and prompting baselines across all settings (e.g., pen-holder SR 8.5→60.3 and CMR 10.5→89.2 in Table 2; leather-bag SR 33.6→89.2 in Table 4; real-world pointing SR 30.0→80.0 in Figure 5).

The error-case analysis (Tables 6/9, Appendix D) is a genuine strength: it decomposes failures into single-view grounding errors, cross-view inconsistency, and manipulation difficulty, and correctly notes that most single-view failures are manipulation-limited rather than prompt-limited. Limitations are discussed honestly rather than hidden.

The appendix meaningfully strengthens the baseline analysis by building a Yo'LLaVA-style token-learning baseline, verifying token-embedding transfer between PaliGemma and the VLA (Table 8), and visualizing induced attention (Figures 9–12).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. VAP is essentially an off-the-shelf pipeline—Grounding DINO detection, DINOv2 crop matching with per-reference top-1 voting, SAM2 segmentation/tracking—plus a template string rewrite. The 'visual attentive prompting' concept is very close to prior visual-prompting / Set-of-Mark / RoboGround-style work, and the paper contributes little new technical insight beyond showing that pixel-space highlighting helps personalization.

The instruction-rewrite design is brittle and unablated. The method uses rigid string matching ('my X' → 'the tint-color X', e.g., 'the red cup'), but it is never explained how the tint color is chosen, whether it is guaranteed unique/descriptive in the scene, or what happens when a distractor shares that color (a real confound). There is no ablation isolating the mask highlight from the instruction rewrite, so the source of the gains is not disentangled.

Baseline fairness. The token-learning (Soft Prompt) baseline is a proxy: concept tokens are learned on a PaliGemma VLM and copied into the VLA, which the authors themselves call an approximation. No baseline is given equivalent test-time grounding (e.g., a location/attribute description derived from the same detector), so the comparison effectively contrasts 'has grounding' against 'lacks grounding' rather than isolating the value of pixel-space prompting.

Metric interpretation is hand-wavy. The recurring high-CMR/low-SR pattern for Soft Prompt is attributed to 'incidental object motion in a tightly cluttered setting' without any verification, and the reliability/validity of CMR as a personalization metric is not established.

Reproducibility is under-addressed. There is no statement that code, checkpoints, or benchmark assets will be released; the benchmarks rely on Sketchfab 3D assets with unclear licensing/availability, and the episode-generation and distractor-selection procedures are only loosely specified (e.g., how 'visually similar' distractors are chosen per category).
Real-world evidence is thin statistically: 20 trials per task (160 total), with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported, making the margins hard to assess.

Some overclaiming and imprecision: the framing as 'top-down selective attention in the cognitive sense' overstates a simple input-preprocessing trick, and notation is inconsistent (the prompting function is defined to output (x̃_t, ℓ̃) but results are reported with hatted symbols).

strengths: Addresses a meaningful and under-explored problem: personalization of frozen VLA policies to user-specific object instances ('my cup') among visually similar distractors, which is practically relevant for home/office assistance.

The proposed VAP pipeline is simple, training-free, and modular, reusing strong off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2) in a coherent grounding-tracking-prompting loop, making deployment immediately feasible after registering a few reference images.

Evaluation is broad and convincing in scope: two new simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER across two embodiments, Personalized-VLABench with multi-view selection) plus a real-world SO-101 setup, with consistent large gains over generic and language/token baselines in both SR and CMR.
The efficiency analysis (Table 5) shows the perception overhead is modest (~10% per step), which strengthens the practical-utility argument for a training-free adapter.

The error-case taxonomy (Table 6/9 and Appendix D) is a genuine strength: it honestly disentangles grounding failures (single-view ambiguity, cross-view inconsistency) from downstream manipulation failures, and the limitations discussion is candid about single-object, short-horizon scope.
The token-embedding-space analysis (Appendix B) is a thoughtful, non-trivial effort to make the Soft Prompt baseline credible rather than a straw man.
weaknesses: The central claim—that visual attentive prompting (the pixel-space highlight) is what enables personalization—is not isolated by ablation. There is no experiment separating the contribution of the highlight from the instruction rewrite, or from grounding/tracking alone (e.g., grounding + rewrite without highlight, or highlight without rewrite). As written, the gains could largely come from the grounding pipeline plus the generic-instruction rewrite, leaving the titular 'visual prompt' contribution unverified.

The baselines are potentially mis-specified in ways that inflate the gap. The Soft Prompt token-learning baseline transfers VLM-learned tokens into a VLA with a separate flow-matching action expert; the paper itself argues this transfer is architecturally awkward, so it may understate what token/conditioning-based personalization could achieve if trained end-to-end in the VLA. Hard/Soft prompt baselines also lack any grounding, making the comparison partly a comparison of grounding vs. no grounding rather than of prompting strategies.

The benchmarks are co-designed with the method: personal objects are instantiated as assets, distractors added, and highlights/tints chosen by the authors. This is reasonable but raises the question of whether the visual highlight is beneficial mainly because the color-tint rewrite ('the red cup') is aligned with the tint used in the prompt; an ablation varying highlight style vs. rewrite style would clarify robustness.

The instruction-rewrite mechanism appears brittle: it relies on template string matching of 'my X' and substituting a tint color, which will fail for non-color-distinguishable instances or instructions not following the 'my X' pattern. No analysis of rewrite failure modes is provided.

Originality is moderate: the individual ingredients (reference-image grounding, visual prompting for robotics, instance matching) exist in prior work (PerSAM, PIN, MOKA, PIVOT, TraceVLA); the contribution is the combination and application, not a new mechanism.

Presentation issues: the prompts in Appendix A.3 are mislabeled (the 'Long Textual Description' prompt requests a 'short noun phrase' while the 'Short Textual Description' prompt requests a 'highly detailed noun phrase'), which is confusing. It is also unclear whether the constructed benchmarks and reference sets will be released, which affects reproducibility of the central claims.

strengths: Well-motivated and timely problem: personalizing frozen VLA models to manipulate user-specific objects among visually similar distractors is important for real-world robotics and is underexplored.

Simple and effective training-free approach: VAP cleverly combines off-the-shelf vision models (Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2) with visual prompting and instruction rewriting, achieving strong gains without per-object fine-tuning.

Comprehensive evaluation: two new simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench) and a real-world tabletop benchmark with multiple robots and tasks, plus comparisons against generic, hard-prompt, and soft-prompt baselines.

Strong empirical results: VAP significantly outperforms baselines in success rate and correct-object manipulation across all benchmarks, with large margins (e.g., 60.3% vs 8.5% SR on pen holder task).
Thorough ablations and error analysis: detailed studies on instruction rewriting, aggregation methods, number of reference images, and prompt design, along with an honest breakdown of failure modes.
Real-world validation on a physical SO-101 robot demonstrates practical applicability and closes the gap between simulation and deployment.
Good presentation: clear figures, tables, and organization, with limitations and future directions discussed extensively in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is a pipeline of existing components (open-vocabulary detection, embedding matching, segmentation, visual prompting) plus a heuristic instruction rewrite; visual prompting for manipulation is not new.

The instruction rewrite relies on a fixed tint color and a simple string template (e.g., 'my cup' -> 'the red cup'), which may not generalize to diverse personalization requests and depends on the VLA's ability to ground color adjectives.

Multi-view inconsistency is a major failure mode (up to 59% of failures in multi-view settings), yet the current per-view independent processing does not address it; the proposed cross-view association remains future work.

The 'training-free' claim is partially misleading because the VLA backbone is fine-tuned for environment adaptation (with generic data) for each new robot/environment, requiring data collection and training overhead.
The use of GPT-5.1 for generating baseline textual descriptions is questionable and unverifiable, potentially affecting reproducibility of the hard-prompt baselines.
Real-world evaluation uses a small number of trials (20 per task), limiting statistical strength and generalizability.

The benchmarks are adaptations of existing ones and use a limited set of instruction templates ('my X'), which may not capture the full diversity of natural personalization requests or long-horizon tasks.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated task formulation: the paper formalizes personal-object manipulation for VLAs, where a frozen policy must act on a user-specific instance among same-category distractors given a few reference images. This extends VLA capabilities from category-level to instance-level grounding and is a genuinely useful problem statement.

Comprehensive evaluation: two newly constructed simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER across Fractal/WidowX, Personalized-VLABench) plus a real-world SO-101 tabletop setup, with several baselines and a broad set of tasks.

Practical, training-free personalization: VAP requires no per-object parameter updates and adds only ~0.02 s/step tracking overhead, which is a meaningful deployment advantage over fine-tuning approaches.

Good empirical discipline: the ablations (mask vs. box, opacity, voting vs. averaging, reference count K) cleanly isolate which components matter, and the error taxonomy (single-view grounding, multi-view inconsistency, control failure) is informative and honest.

Thorough analysis of the token-learning baseline, including embedding-space transfer metrics (cosine/CKA/kNN) and attention visualizations, which strengthens the comparison rather than relying on a single number.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: VAP is essentially an off-the-shelf pipeline (Grounding DINO + DINOv2 matching + SAM2 tracking) combined with a colored-mask overlay and a template instruction rewrite ('my X' -> 'the [tint-color] X'). There is no new learning, algorithm, or theoretical insight; the core 'trick' is a simple heuristic, which is thin for a top-tier ML venue.

Baseline concerns: no comparison to reference-conditioned / in-context VLA personalization methods (e.g., RICL, which is cited but not evaluated). The Soft-Prompt baseline is a proxy transferred from a frozen VLM rather than a native VLA personalization method, so the reported margins may overstate the advantage.

Unresolved multi-view failure mode: the paper's own error analysis shows 50-60% of multi-view failures come from cross-view inconsistency (Case 2), which the authors explicitly defer to future work. Since multi-view is the realistic deployment setting, this is a substantial unaddressed limitation of the proposed method.

Narrow instantiation of the rewrite: a fixed template and a fixed tint color are used, and generalization to arbitrary phrasings, languages, or categories the detector cannot recognize is not demonstrated. The grounding also depends on the category name being detectable by the open-vocabulary detector.

Statistical rigor of the real-world study: results are over only ~20 trials/task, and the reported error bars are computed across the four tasks rather than per task, which is not a meaningful uncertainty estimate for the central real-world claims.
Reproducibility: no clear statement of code/benchmark release; benchmarks rely on Sketchfab assets and specific physical objects on a particular robot, making independent reproduction difficult.
Framing nuance: the 'training-free' claim refers only to personalization, while the backbone VLA is fine-tuned per environment; this should be stated more prominently to avoid overstating generality.

strengths: The paper formulates a clear and practically important problem: personal object manipulation for VLAs, where a frozen policy must identify and act on a user-specific instance among visually similar distractors using only a few reference images.

VAP is a simple, training-free input-side adapter that couples reference-based instance grounding (open-vocabulary detection, DINOv2 matching, SAM2 tracking) with a mask-aligned visual highlight and instruction rewrite. It requires no per-object parameter updates and adds only 0.02 s per control step, preserving real-time responsiveness.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this setting: two adapted simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER across Google Robot and WidowX, Personalized-VLABench on Franka) and a real-world SO-101 tabletop benchmark with eight tasks, multiple backbones (π0, π0.5), and both success rate and correct movement ratio metrics.

The baselines are thoughtfully constructed and strong, including generic VLA, short/long hard textual prompts generated from reference images, and a Yo’LLaVA-style token-learning baseline trained with oracle hard negatives and achieving >95% VQA recognition. The token embedding analysis in Appendix B further strengthens the comparison.

Ablations isolate key design choices: mask + rewrite vs mask-only/rewrite-only, voting vs averaging, number of reference images K, and mask vs bounding-box prompting with varying opacity. These support the central claims about the importance of coupled visual and language prompting.

The error analysis is honest and informative, explicitly identifying multi-view inconsistency as a major failure mode in multi-camera settings and separating grounding failures from downstream control failures. The limitations discussion is concrete and points to meaningful future work.

The paper provides substantial reproducibility details: hardware and software setup, training data construction, hyperparameters, instruction rewriting logic, object descriptions, and runtime profiling.

The method is significant as a practical bridge between semantic category-level VLA generalization and instance-level personalization, and the real-world demonstration on physical hardware strengthens the practical relevance.
weaknesses: There are notable inconsistencies in episode-count reporting across tables. For example, Table 1 lists 96 episodes for Personalized-SIMPLER (Bridge), while Table 3 says each task is evaluated with 10 runs of 24 episodes (240 per task), and Table 6 lists 96 × 10. Similarly, Table 1 lists 250 episodes for Personalized-VLABench, Table 4 says 10 runs of 50 episodes per task, and Table 6 reports 125 × 10. These inconsistencies hinder reproducibility and make it difficult to interpret the scale of the evaluation.

The simulation results generally lack statistical significance tests or confidence intervals. Some claimed gains are modest in Personalized-VLABench (e.g., shoe: 54.0 vs 52.0 for Hard Prompt Short; cat figurine: 51.6 vs 44.4 for Soft Prompt), so the repeated use of “significantly” is not fully supported by formal analysis.

The instruction rewriting is a rigid template: it assumes a “my X” span and replaces it with “the tint-color X.” This limits natural-language generality, may fail for multi-object or more complex instructions, and relies on a fixed tint color whose interaction with object color and other colored objects is not systematically ablated.

Multi-view inconsistency is a major unresolved failure mode: 59.2% of Personalized-VLABench failures and 50.9% of real-world failures are attributed to contradictory per-view prompts. The current per-view factorization therefore remains a significant weakness in multi-camera settings, even if honestly reported.

The method depends heavily on off-the-shelf open-vocabulary detection and segmentation. There is no robustness evaluation under detector/segmenter failures, calibration errors, severe occlusion, or adversarial distractors, so the boundary conditions of the approach remain unclear.

The benchmarks are newly constructed by the authors. Although adapted from existing simulators and evaluated on real hardware, the lack of a public release or independent validation raises questions about potential selection bias in object sets, reference images, distractor difficulty, and task design.

The “training-free” claim is somewhat nuanced: the backbone π0.5 is fine-tuned for environment adaptation on generic data before VAP is applied. While no per-object training is used, the paper should more clearly scope this additional training step when discussing training-free personalization.

The semi-transparent tint overlays the target region and may obscure fine visual details needed for precise grasping or placement. The opacity ablation is useful but does not fully characterize this tradeoff across all manipulation tasks, especially contact-rich pick-and-place scenarios.
